completion:
The law of iterated expectations (also called the law of total expectation) states that if \(X\) and \(Y\) are random variables for which the relevant expectations exist, then
\[
\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[X \mid Y]] = \mathbb{E}[X].
\]
To see why this identity holds, begin with the definition of conditional expectation. The random variable \(\mathbb{E}[X \mid Y]\) is a (measurable) function of \(Y\), say \(g(Y)\), that satisfies
\[
\int_{B} g(Y) \, dP = \int_{B} X \, dP
\]
for every event \(B\) belonging to the \(\sigma\)-algebra generated by \(Y\). Taking the expectation of both sides (i.e., integrating over the whole sample space) immediately yields
\[
\mathbb{E}[g(Y)] = \mathbb{E}[X],
\]
which is precisely the claimed identity.

The same conclusion can be reached by writing the expectation in terms of the joint density (or mass function) when it exists:
\[
\mathbb{E}[X] = \iint x f_{X,Y}(x,y) \, dx \, dy = \int \Bigl( \int x f_{X \mid Y}(x \mid y) \, dx \Bigr) f_Y(y) \, dy = \int \mathbb{E}[X \mid Y=y] f_Y(y) \, dy = \mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[X \mid Y]].
\]
Thus \(\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[X \mid Y]]\) equals the unconditional expectation of \(X\).

Among the given choices, only option (C) matches this result. Option (A) is a random variable, not a constant; options (B) and (D) have no general relationship to the iterated expectation.

FINAL_ANSWER: C

Binary search is an algorithm whose correctness and \(O(\log n)\) worst-case complexity both rely on two prerequisites that must be satisfied simultaneously:

- The collection must already be sorted in ascending order.

Now consider each option:
